cases.user_message:
Спорим с братом уже час, рассудите. Игра: 4 закрытые двери, за одной приз, за тремя пусто. Я выбираю дверь №1. Ведущий НЕ знает, где приз, — он просто наугад открывает одну из трёх оставшихся дверей (№2, №3 или №4). В нашем случае он открыл №3, и там оказалось пусто. Теперь мне предлагают либо остаться на №1, либо перейти на одну из двух оставшихся закрытых дверей (№2 или №4, выбираю любую из них).

Брат говорит: это как задача Монти Холла, менять выгоднее, у №1 шанс 1/4, а у каждой из двух других 3/8. А мне кажется, что раз ведущий открывал наугад, это уже не то же самое. Кто прав? Дайте конкретные вероятности для каждой двери.
cases.why_in_scope: The implant makes the model work the problem along several separate lines (Bayes' rule, counting equally likely outcomes, comparison with the host-knows version) and check that they agree before answering. The brother's 1/4 vs 3/8 is the right answer for a host who knows where the prize is, and a strong model that recognises the Monty Hall pattern can repeat it after a short argument. Here the host picks at random, so all three closed doors have probability 1/3.
rubric: States that, given the host opened door 3 at random and it was empty, door 1 and doors 2 and 4 each have probability 1/3, so switching gives no advantage.
Says the brother's 1/4 and 3/8 figures apply only when the host knows where the prize is and always opens an empty door.

Shows the conditioning step explicitly, e.g. the chance the host's random pick reveals an empty door is 1 if the prize is behind door 1 and 2/3 otherwise, giving (1/4) / (1/4 + 3/4 * 2/3) = 1/3 for door 1.
Checks the result a second way (e.g. by counting equally likely host-choice/prize cases or by checking that the probabilities sum to 1).

cases.user_message:
Settling a question for a board game I'm designing. A player rolls a fair six-sided die repeatedly and stops as soon as they roll a 6. The turn only counts as a "clean run" if every roll in the turn, including the final 6, was even (so any 1, 3 or 5 along the way spoils it).

I want the average turn length among clean runs only. My co-designer says it's obviously 3: if only 2, 4, 6 are allowed, it's like rolling a 3-sided die until you hit the 6, so the expected length is 3. That seems right to me but the playtest numbers look lower. Is 3 correct? If not, what's the exact value and why is the 3-sided-die argument wrong?
cases.why_in_scope: The co-designer's argument of 3 is the obvious short answer, and many strong models accept it after a one-line check. The implant has the model work the problem more than one way (a direct sum over turn lengths, a conditional-probability argument) and verify it, and those ways show the correct value is 3/2. The model should also explain that conditioning on an all-even turn favours short turns.
rubric: Gives the exact expected clean-run length as 3/2 (1.5), not 3.

Explains why the 3-sided-die argument fails: conditioning on no odd rolls is not the same as removing odd faces from the die, because longer turns are much more likely to include an odd roll, so the condition favours short turns.
Supports the value with an explicit calculation, e.g. P(clean run of length n) = (1/3)^(n-1) * (1/6), so the length given a clean run is geometric with success probability 2/3 and mean 3/2.

Cross-checks the 3/2 result by a second independent route or sanity check (e.g. P(clean run) = 1/4 overall, or the conditional length probabilities 2/3, 2/9, ... summing to 1), and notes that it is consistent with the lower playtest numbers.

checker_notes: Case 1: removed 'подвох' (a trigger phrase of the implant) from the user message and made the conditioning rubric item wording precise. Case 2: replaced the trivial 'playtest consistent' rubric item with a cross-check item targeting the implant's verify-by-another-chain behaviour; verified all numeric claims (1/3 each; 3/2, P(clean)=1/4).
